Never. The premise is false: glass is an amorphous solid, not a slow-flowing liquid, and at room temperature its relaxation time is far longer than the age of the universe. Your windows won't sag.

Old panes are uneven because of how they were made. Crown glass was spun into discs, producing varying thickness, and glaziers often installed the thicker edge down for stability. Cylinder-blown glass was also uneven. Plenty of old windows are thicker at the top or sides, and medieval glass that is thicker at the bottom is a mix of manufacturing and placement. Evidence against flow: ancient optical lenses and Roman glass objects keep their shapes after thousands of years, and old telescope lenses show no deformation.

Modern float glass is flat to a tight tolerance and will stay that way. Visible distortion in your windows would come from thermal stress, failed seals in double-glazing, or frame settling, not from flow.
